pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6: read and WRITE numerals 0–20 — connecting the spoken number, the quantity, and the written symbol. This is the most central node of the whole domain (centrality 0.59): the symbolic gateway everything else builds on.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words' and 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.3 'write numbers 0–20; represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–20'.
• Operational details — the child must (i) recognise/name each numeral on sight, (ii) form each numeral legibly (a handwriting/motor skill), and (iii) map a numeral to a quantity and back. Rests on cardinality (a numeral names a total) and digit-formation. Watch the classic teen reversals and the say-it-as-you-hear-it trap (writing 'twelve' as 21, 'thirteen' as 31) that come from left-to-right speech vs place-value writing.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read any numeral 0–20 shown. Tier B (5–6): write numerals 0–20 legibly from dictation, correct orientation. Tier C (6): shown a set of objects, write the matching numeral, and shown a numeral, make/point to that many.
bestPractices: Keep the numeral tied to QUANTITY at all times — read/write the symbol beside a set of objects, a ten-frame, or fingers — so 0–20 are symbols FOR amounts, not decorations; grounds in cardinality (prerequisite mt_dmNvjroCPT).

Treat numeral formation as an explicit motor skill: model stroke order, use sky-writing/sand/whiteboards, and directly address reversals (2, 5, 7, 9) and the b/d-style confusions with multisensory tracing.

Confront the teen 'hear-it-write-it' trap head-on: 'thirteen' SOUNDS like three-then-ten but is written 13 (ten then three) — pair the spoken word with a ten-frame showing a full ten and 3 more, and with the written 13.
Use frequent read↔write↔represent switching (numeral card → make the set; set → write the numeral; hear it → write it) so all three modes are linked, not siloed.
Include 0 deliberately as 'none' and as a written symbol — many children can count but hesitate to read or write zero.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame(s) beside the numeral (a full ten + extras for teens) linking symbol to a structured quantity.
Numeral formation cards with directional arrows / stroke-order guides for handwriting.
Number track / 0–20 washing-line pairing each numeral with its position and a matching set.
Numeral ↔ objects ↔ spoken-word matching cards (three-way correspondence).
commonMisconceptions: Digit reversals (2, 3, 5, 7, 9 written mirror-image) — a formation issue needing direct correction.
Teen transposition from speech: writing 'thirteen' as 31, 'fourteen' as 41 (hearing the ones first).
Reading a numeral without connecting it to a quantity (naming '7' but unable to make seven).
Confusing visually similar numerals (6/9, 2/5, 7/1) or omitting/misreading 0.
Treating a two-digit teen numeral as two separate single digits (reading 15 as 'one, five').

learn.summary: Children aged 5–6 learn to read and write numerals 0–20, connecting the spoken number word, the quantity, and the written symbol. This is a foundational symbolic skill requiring numeral recognition on sight, legible numeral formation (a handwriting/motor skill), and two-way mapping between a numeral and a quantity. Teaching keeps numerals tied to amounts, treats digit formation as an explicit motor skill, and directly confronts the teen 'hear-it-write-it' transposition trap (writing 'thirteen' as 31) and classic digit reversals.

activities.title: Numeral studio: trace, build the quantity, self-correct
feedback: If a digit is mirror-reversed (e.g. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 written backwards), treat it as a handwriting/formation issue, not a maths error — give stroke-order cues and multisensory tracing (sand, sky-writing) and let it resolve with practice.
If the written numeral doesn't match the set, recount the set together (one tag per object, the last word tells how many) and then write that numeral — don't reteach numeral forms.
When a quantity and its numeral are shown side by side, invite the child to point to 'the full ten and the extra ones' for teens so the symbol maps to the structure.
activities.rationale: Reading and writing numerals is an active symbol↔quantity mapping plus a tracing/formation skill. Keeping the numeral beside a structured quantity (ten-frame, fingers, counters) grounds it in cardinality, and read↔write↔represent switching prevents the modes from being siloed. A guided path makes stroke order and reversal correction concrete, but a fixed chart or paper tracing with adult feedback can serve the same purpose. No cited source directly establishes this pedagogy; it is a research-informed proposal.
learnerActions: Trace a numeral along a guided stroke-order path (start dot and directional arrows) on a whiteboard, in sand, by sky-writing, or on a coded surface that models stroke order.
As the numeral is formed, build or watch a ten-frame fill to that many (using a second ten-frame for 11–20), so the symbol is felt as a quantity rather than a squiggle.
Flip the task: tap/lay out a set of counters, then write or select the numeral that names how many.
Switch frequently between the modes — numeral card → make the set; set → write the numeral; hear it → write it — so reading, writing and representing stay linked.
activities.intendedInsight: A numeral is a symbol FOR a quantity, written and read, not a decoration; the three modes (spoken word, quantity, written symbol) are one connected idea.

activities.title: Hear it, write it: addressing the teen transposition
feedback: Writing a teen in spoken order (41 for 'fourteen', 71 for 'seventeen') is a normal transcription stage that fades as teen place value matures — do NOT drill it as careless or mark it repeatedly wrong. Keep modelling with a ten-and-ones frame.
Read a teen numeral back as a whole number ('fifteen'), not 'one, five', to counter reading a two-digit teen as two separate single digits.
Contrast visually similar numerals (6/9, 2/5, 7/1) by naming each beside its matching set when confusion appears.
activities.rationale: The spoken word order for teens conflicts with written place-value order, causing transposition errors; linking the numeral, the word, and a ten-structured quantity is a recognised way to mitigate this. Showing that 31 would demand three tens and one more gives the child a quantity-grounded self-check rather than a rule to memorise; the check depends on a display that visibly breaks for 31 and is a cue the child performs, not an automatic correction.
sourceClaims: Teen numbers are a known difficulty because the spoken word order (e.g. 'thir-teen') conflicts with the written place-value order, causing transposition errors; linking numeral, word and a ten-structured quantity mitigates this.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken teen word, e.g. 'thirteen', and see two ten-frames: one FULL frame of ten and a second frame with 3 more.
Write the numeral by forming the ten digit first and then the ones digit: 1 then 3.
Check: if you write 31, the quantity would need three full tens and one more, which cannot match the single full ten and three extras shown.
Repeat with 'fourteen', 'seventeen', 'nineteen', pairing the spoken word, the ten-structured quantity, and the written numeral each time.
Include 0 deliberately — say 'none', show an empty frame, and read and write the symbol 0.
activities.intendedInsight: The words for 13–19 say the ones first ('thir-teen') but the numerals are written ten-then-ones (13); eleven and twelve do not follow this pattern. Pairing the word with a full-ten-plus-extras quantity shows why 13, not 31, is correct.

activities.title: Read-and-match reference wall and checks
feedback: Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition but do not by themselves require the child to form a numeral — follow a correct match with an actual writing of the numeral.
If a child names a numeral but cannot make that many, return to building the set beside the symbol before moving on.
For a dictation check such as 'write fourteen, seventeen, twelve, nineteen', watch the teens especially, then ask the child to make a counted set (e.g. 16 counters) and write how many.
activities.rationale: Recognition and matching are cleanly assessable, and a tap-to-hear reference wall is a useful support, but recognition-only or matching-only responses do not elicit independent numeral formation, which is half the objective. These activities are best used to check and reinforce alongside, not instead of, actual writing.
learnerActions: Use a 0–20 number track or washing-line pairing each numeral with its position and a matching set; tap or point to a numeral to hear its name and reveal a matching ten-frame display (two frames for 11–20).
Match numeral cards to sets or ten-frames (three-way: numeral ↔ objects ↔ spoken word).
Given a shown or spoken quantity, pick or write the matching numeral, including deliberate 12/21-style distractors to probe the teen trap.
Trace a dictated numeral along a path to check formation.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and matching numerals to quantities is a distinct, checkable layer that should always reconnect the symbol to an amount and, where possible, to writing it.

constraints: Numeral writing (actual formation of each digit) is half the objective — matching, multiple-choice and tap-to-reveal reference activities test or support recognition but do not themselves require numeral formation and must not fully replace writing.
Always keep the numeral tied to a quantity (ten-frame, fingers, counters) so 0–20 are symbols for amounts, not decorations; grounds in cardinality (a prerequisite).
Treat digit reversals (commonly 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9) as a handwriting/formation issue needing stroke-order cues, not as a number error.
Treat teen transposition (41 for 'fourteen') as a normal developmental transcription stage; keep modelling the ten-and-ones structure rather than drilling or repeatedly marking it wrong.
Include 0 deliberately as 'none' and as a written symbol, since many children can count but hesitate to read or write zero.
A tap-to-hear numeral chart or number track is a useful reference but cannot capture the child forming numerals; use it as support alongside writing practice.

Stroke-order paths, reversal-blocking pens, live ten-frame fills and drag-to-match are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory, and paper, sand, whiteboards and counters with adult feedback can serve the same goals.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims for CCSS-M K.CC.3 and the NCETM teen-difficulty guidance were marked verified:false in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.

The original recommendation asserted an open in-role dialogue 'cannot teach numeral formation' and that a 3D environment 'adds nothing'. These are comparative/necessity claims not established by the sources; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (recognition vs formation) rather than universal laws. A fixed chart or non-interactive medium can still support recognition.

The claim that writing 31 for thirteen 'self-corrects' because the quantity would need three tens assumes a ten-frame display that visibly breaks for 31; this is a design-dependent cue, not an automatic correction, and is presented as a check the child performs.

sourceClaims were tightened so each cites only a claim that supports the activity's teaching principle. The NCETM teen-difficulty claim is retained for activity[1] (it directly supports linking numeral, word and quantity to reduce transposition). K.CC.3 was removed from activity[0] because it documents the curriculum objective rather than the activity's pedagogy (cardinality grounding and read↔write↔represent switching); activity[0] therefore has no directly supporting claim, and activity[2]'s recognition-vs-formation affordance likewise has none, so both use [].

probeDeeper: Write the number that comes after 12.
Show me 14 with counters, then write it — do they match?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads all correctly; writes 14, 17, 12, 19; writes 16 for the set — with teens not reversed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes teen numbers in spoken order: 41 for 'fourteen', 71 for 'seventeen' (hears the ones word first)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill it as a careless mistake or mark it repeatedly wrong — it is a normal transcription stage that fades as teen place value matures. Keep modelling with a ten-and-ones frame.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictated teens come out reversed while single digits and 'twelve/twenty' may be fine.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat as handwriting, not maths — don't count it as a number error; give formation cues and let it resolve with writing practice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digits are recognisable but flipped left-right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes a numeral that doesn't match the counted quantity (miscounts the set)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach numeral forms — recount the set together (one tag per object, last word = how many) then write that.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written numeral is off by one or two from the actual count of counters.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot read or write numerals 0–20 reliably, or the numeral doesn't match a counted set.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes all numerals 0–20 from sight and dictation and matches a numeral to a counted quantity.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most, but teens are occasionally reversed or a digit mirror-formed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch the child read and write. 'Read these: 7, 13, 15, 11, 20. Now write these as I say them: fourteen, seventeen, twelve, nineteen.' Then: 'Here are 16 counters — write how many.' Watch the teens especially.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Dictating teens catches the transposition stage (41 for fourteen); a counted set checks the numeral is tied to quantity, not just copied. Watching the writing distinguishes a genuine gap from a normal formation/reversal stage.
